𝐍𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐰𝐥𝐞𝐫, 𝟐𝟎𝟏𝟒.⁣
⁣
I’ll never forget the first time I saw Nightcrawler (2014). It was late, the streets outside were dead quiet, and I had that weird buzzing feeling you get when you’re too awake to sleep but too tired to think. Perfect conditions to meet Louis Bloom. And Jake Gyllenhaal, bug-eyed and terrifyingly thin, crawled right into my brain and didn’t leave for days.⁣
⁣
Once he signed on to this role, I knew it’d be special. Gyllenhaal had already been on a streak (Zodiac, Prisoners, Enemy) but this was different. He went all in. Every sleazy smirk, every flat, rehearsed monologue, every wide-eyed stare that looked like he hadn’t blinked in hours. The man turned himself into a worm, a nightcrawler, squirming through the gutters of Los Angeles chasing the next bloody shot. And the terrifying part? You believe him.⁣
⁣
On paper, Nightcrawler (2014) is about a thief who stumbles into the world of freelance crime journalism. Basically an ambulance-chaser with a camera. But Dan Gilroy, in his directorial debut no less, transforms it into a dark mirror. It’s Drive’s slick neon style fused with Network’s media satire, only nastier. We watch Lou hustle his way from petty thief to professional sociopath, selling carnage to Rene Russo’s ruthless news director, pushing boundaries until there are no boundaries left. ⁣
⁣
This movie is unsettling but also funny as f*k. Lou’s complete lack of shame. The way he negotiates with dead-eyed persistence. The absurdly polite way he talks while saying the most manipulative crap... What fascinates me most is that Lou isn’t the “bad guy” in the traditional sense. He’s the protagonist. We’re stuck with him. Forced to follow him. It’s intoxicating. You don’t root for him, but you can’t wait to see how far he’ll go. It’s Rupert Pupkin by way of Patrick Bateman, delusional and smiling, convinced he’s the hero of his own story.

source_details.synopsis: Nightcrawler is a 2014 American satirical, psychological thriller film written and directed by Dan Gilroy in his directorial debut. It stars Jake Gyllenhaal as an unhinged stringer who seeks out violent and morbid events late at night in Los Angeles so he can film them and sell the exclusive footage to a local television news station. The supporting cast includes Rene Russo, Riz Ahmed, and Bill Paxton. Gilroy originally wanted to make a film about the life of the American photographer Weegee, but switched focus after discovering the unique narrative possibilities surrounding the stringer profession.
